name: Negativity bias
statement: Negative information is said to weigh more than positive information of the same size, a principle usually summarised as bad is stronger than good.
meaning: Three claims travel under one name and rest on different literatures. The first is about weighting: negative information counts for more than positive information when someone forms an impression. The second is about duration: bad events leave affective consequences that outlast good ones of matching size. The third is about the body: negative material draws a larger physiological response. Rozin and Royzman cut the idea a fourth way, into negative potency, steeper negative gradients, negativity dominance and negative differentiation. Negativity dominance is their sharpest version, that a mixture of good and bad is judged worse than the sum of its parts. Support for any one of these is routinely reported as support for all of them.

origin.who: Roy F. Baumeister, Ellen Bratslavsky, Catrin Finkenauer and Kathleen D. Vohs
origin.note: "Bad Is Stronger Than Good" ran to 48 pages and gathered findings from everyday events, trauma, close relationships, social networks and learning. Rozin and Royzman published their taxonomy in Personality and Social Psychology Review a month earlier, in November 2001, and Baumeister and colleagues cite it as in press. Neither paper coined the phenomenon; both were attempts to give a scattered literature one name.

evidence: Both founding statements are reviews rather than meta-analyses, and Baumeister and colleagues set their own method apart from both. They write that "Unlike more focused narrative reviews or meta-analyses, we were unable to conduct a systematic search using keywords such as good or bad". A request to the Society for Personality and Social Psychology list-serve drew roughly 100 replies, and those replies were the starting point for the search. They also state their priority plainly: "The consistency of conclusions across each area is more important than the robustness or methodological strength of evidence in each specific area." Their abstract concludes that hardly any exceptions, meaning findings of greater power of good, can be found. Rozin and Royzman draw on literary, historical, religious and cultural material alongside psychological work on learning, attention, impression formation, contagion, moral judgement, development and memory. Neither review reports a pooled effect size. Brannon and Gawronski, surveying the same field in 2018, name Pratto and John's automatic-vigilance work as the standard attention demonstration and Kanouse and Hanson as the standard impression-formation one.

replication.headline: A registered report on 12,448 randomised headline tests found negative words raise clicks, while three well-powered experiments found no negativity bias in impression formation.
replication.detail: The strongest test is a registered report whose stage 1 protocol was accepted in March 2022. Robertson, Pröllochs, Schwarzenegger, Pärnamets, Van Bavel and Feuerriegel analysed the confirmatory half of the Upworthy Research Archive. It holds 22,743 randomised trials in which rival headlines for the same story were served to real readers between January 2013 and April 2015, drawing about 5.7 million clicks across more than 370 million impressions. Preregistered filtering left 12,448 trials and 53,699 headlines, the number the paper's regression table reports as its observation count. Its figure captions give 53,669 for the same quantity, and the paper does not reconcile the two. A larger proportion of negative words raised the odds of a click, beta = 0.015, SE = 0.001, z = 17.42, 99% CI [0.013, 0.018]. For a headline of average length, close to 15 words, each negative word lifted the click-through rate by 2.3 percent. Each positive word cut it by about 1.0 percent, beta = -0.008, SE = 0.001, z = -9.24, 99% CI [-0.010, -0.006]. Two preregistered emotion predictions failed. Fear ran opposite to the prediction, and an equivalence test on anger was undecided at p = 0.399. The physiological claim holds on average and comes apart at the level of the person. Soroka, Fournier and Nir ran one protocol on 1,156 respondents in 17 countries across six continents, recording heart-rate variability and skin conductance while people watched real video news. Shifting story tone from positive to negative moved heart-rate variability by 10 percent of its observed standard deviation, and skin conductance measured 20 seconds into a story by 65 percent. Taken country by country, the mean coefficient cleared zero on a one-tailed test in 5 of 17 countries for heart-rate variability and 9 of 17 for skin conductance. In New Zealand and Sweden the skin-conductance effect ran the other way, though not reliably. Country explains 1.5 percent of the variance in individual coefficients for heart-rate variability and 2.7 percent for skin conductance, so the spread sits between people rather than between cultures. The impression-formation claim fares worse. Brannon and Gawronski ran three experiments with 972 participants testing whether new negative information violates an expectancy more than new positive information does. It did not, and the amount of prior information about the target made no difference. On duration, Luhmann, Hofmann, Eid and Lucas pooled 313 samples and 65,911 people across marriage, divorce, bereavement, childbirth, unemployment, reemployment, retirement and relocation. They report that the effects of life events on wellbeing "are not a function of the alleged desirability of events", which cuts against ranking events by how bad they were.

study.cite: Robertson, C. E., Pröllochs, N., Schwarzenegger, K., Pärnamets, P., Van Bavel, J. J., & Feuerriegel, S. (2023). Negativity drives online news consumption. Nature Human Behaviour, 7(5), 812-822.

limits: The verdict covers the general principle rather than any one of its parts, and the parts do not move together. Negative language raising news consumption is preregistered and it held. Greater physiological response to negative news held on average across 17 countries and did not reach conventional levels in most of them taken singly. Negative information dominating impression formation did not appear in a 972-participant study designed to find it. Searches of Crossref, Europe PMC and the journals turned up no Many Labs or multi-laboratory replication of the negativity bias itself; the preregistered evidence found here tests headline clicks, not the laboratory paradigms the 2001 reviews were built from. The idea also carries weight in political science. Hibbing, Smith and Alford argued in a Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article that negativity bias is the organising element behind the liberal-conservative divide, with conservatives registering greater physiological and psychological responses to negative features of the environment. The study behind that claim is Oxley and colleagues' 2008 report in Science. Bakker, Schumacher, Gothreau and Arceneaux ran a preregistered direct replication of it with 202 participants, plus conceptual replications with 352 in the United States and 81 in the Netherlands. Their analyses did not support the original conclusions, and they found no evidence for the broader claims about disgust or about a physiological trait. Corns argues the principle should be rejected as ill-formed, because strength is measured as duration, ease of learning, speed of processing and emotional impact by turns, and opposite results are read as support for the same hypothesis. Unkelbach, Alves and Koch offer a rival account in which positive information is simply more alike than negative information, so valence asymmetries follow from the structure of the environment with no processing bias behind them. Freyer and colleagues formalise both positions and conclude that a theory must say what counts as good and what counts as bad before a test of it can be informative.
misreadings: The 2001 papers are cited as though they were meta-analyses. They are not, and Baumeister and colleagues describe their own search as unsystematic and their emphasis as breadth rather than methodological strength. The second error is treating negativity bias as one effect with one effect size. Attention, impression formation, affective duration and physiological arousal are separate claims, and the evidence for them now points in different directions. The third is reading the cross-national result as a universal. Soroka, Fournier and Nir report an average negativity bias and also report that most of their 17 country samples would not show one alone. Their own conclusion is that the result gives reason to reconsider the journalistic maxim that if it bleeds, it leads. The fourth is treating negativity dominance as established because negative news gets clicked. Robertson and colleagues measured a behaviour, the click, and note that a preference for negative headlines does not show that readers felt worse.
